Figure 4-1 compares the distribution of the fuel costs ($/ton-miles) for each of the biofuel options. In the figure, for the sake of comparison, we added conventional diesel fuel cost and LCO for battery-electric locomotives and hydrogen fuel cell locomotives. The cost estimates for battery-electric locomotives and hydrogen locomotives are collected from Hernandez et al. (2021). Figure 4-1 Levelized Cost of Operation (in $/ton-mile) for Different Alternative Fuels Figure 4-1 shows that, based on the fuel cost estimates for different routes, methanol has the lowest average cost (around $0.0045/ton-mile). Although methanol does not have the lowest MFSP among all biofuel options that we considered, the high mix ratio (95% by volume) seems to play a vital role in reducing the cost. All three drop-in biofuels—BD100, RD100, and biodiesel blend (BD20 + RD80)—have very similar estimated average costs (around 0.005$/ton-mile). This is due to the similarity in MSFP for BD (from soybean) and RD (from biomass CFP). 4.2 CASE STUDY: INTERMODAL TRAINS BETWEEN CHICAGO AND LOS ANGELES We evaluated a case study on intermodal trains operating on the Burlington-Northern Santa Fe southern transcontinental route between Chicago and Los Angeles. We simulated four types of intermodal trains: international stack, domestic stack, TOFC (trailer on flat car), and a container- trailer mixed train. Table 4-3 presents the fuel consumption and energy intensity for four types of intermodal trains across both directions of the southern transcontinental route. The average energy intensity is 772 Btu/revenue ton-mile. Container-based intermodal trains exhibit the highest energy intensity, followed by mixed container and trailer intermodal, with trailer-based intermodal trains 28 having the lowest. Because grades are slightly steeper, energy intensity is higher for all intermodal types when travelling from Los Angeles to Chicago than from Chicago to Los Angeles.
